title: The Primary and Secondary Corporate Credit Facilities

source.name: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

summary: This New York Fed Economic Policy Review article examines the design, operations, and impact of the Primary Market Corporate Credit Facility (PMCCF) and Secondary Market Corporate Credit Facility (SMCCF), the Federal Reserve's first-ever intervention in corporate bond markets. The facilities were launched in March 2020 to address severe dislocations in the $9.6 trillion corporate bond market during the COVID-19 pandemic, when yield spreads widened approximately 250 bps for investment-grade and 550 bps for high-yield bonds. The SMCCF made total purchases of $14 billion before ceasing operations on December 31, 2020.
key_points: PMCCF and SMCCF were announced March 23, 2020, authorized under Section 13(3) of the Federal Reserve Act to support market functioning for corporate bonds and syndicated loans
SMCCF commenced ETF purchases on May 12, 2020, and direct bond purchases on June 16, 2020; PMCCF became operational June 29, 2020 but was never used by a borrower
In the last two weeks of March 2020, corporate bond mutual funds and ETFs experienced approximately $200 billion in outflows
New issue concessions widened to more than 50 bps above secondary market yields, approximately double the usual spread; high-yield issuance halted almost entirely between March 4 and April 16, 2020
SMCCF ceased purchases December 31, 2020 with total purchases of $14 billion; portfolio wind-down completed August 31, 2021
The authors show that the announcement of the program had a dramatic effect on liquidity and pricing in the secondary market while also reigniting issuance in the primary market
why_it_matters: This paper provides the Federal Reserve's own analysis of its unprecedented direct intervention in corporate bond markets. Understanding the design, usage, and impact of the PMCCF/SMCCF is essential for assessing potential future Fed tools for addressing corporate credit market dislocations. The analysis demonstrates how forward guidance about backstop facilities can restore market functioning without requiring large actual purchases.
macro_context: The CCFs were designed to support credit provision to the nonfinancial corporate sector and prevent forced defaults by solvent corporations unable to refinance maturing debt. The facilities also supported bank lending by reducing liquidity demands when bond issuers pre-emptively drew down revolving credit lines.
market_structure_context: This paper is directly relevant to market structure as it analyzes the Federal Reserve's first direct purchases of corporate bonds and ETFs, changes in bid-ask spreads and liquidity measures during the crisis, and the role of dealer markets and OTC trading in corporate bonds. It examines how the facilities restored market functioning and reignited primary market issuance.
important_numbers: $9.6 trillion in corporate debt securities outstanding (end of 2019)
250 bps increase in investment-grade yield spreads
550 bps increase in high-yield yield spreads
$200 billion in outflows from corporate bond funds (last two weeks March 2020)
50 bps+ new issue concession (approximately double normal)
